english: Where do you transfer?
tip: 갈아타요 (garatayo = transfer) splits into 갈아 (gara = change) + 타다 (tada = ride) – literally 'change-ride', which is exactly what a transfer is.

english: I transfer at Gangnam Station.
tip: Transferring is 'change-riding': 갈아타요 (garatayo) = 갈다 (change) + 타다 (ride). Korean fuses the two verbs into one word.

english: Do you have a T-money card?
tip: Korean has no 'have' – things just exist to you: 티머니 카드가 있어요 (timeoni kadeuga isseoyo) is literally 'a T-money card exists'. 있다 covers both 'there is' and 'I have'.

english: Yesterday I loaded 10,000 won onto it.
tip: Korean counts big numbers in ten-thousands: 만 원 (man won) = 10,000 won in one syllable. 만 is its own unit – not built as ten × thousand the way English says it.

english: The subway is faster than the bus.
tip: 보다 (boda) after a noun means 'than': 버스보다 빨라요 (beoseuboda ppallayo = faster than the bus). The thing you compare against carries the marker, not the subject.

english: At rush hour there are so many people.
tip: Korean says 'people are many', not 'there are many people': 사람이 정말 많아요 (sarami jeongmal manayo). The describing verb 많다 (manta) does all the work.

english: I missed the last train.
tip: 놓치다 (nochida = miss) is for things that get away – 막차를 놓쳤어요 (makchareul nochyeosseoyo). Missing a person uses a completely different verb.

english: The next bus comes in ten minutes.
tip: 'After' comes after: 10분 후에 (sip-bun hue) is literally '10 minutes after-at'. 후 follows the time span instead of leading it like English 'in ten minutes'.

english: There were no seats.
tip: 'There weren't any' is one verb: 자리가 없었어요 (jariga eopseosseoyo) = 'seats not-existed'. 없다 packs 'not' and 'exist' together – no separate negative word.

english: It's 1,500 won.
tip: Korean drops the 'one': 1,500 is 천오백 (cheonobaek), not 일천오백. 천 (cheon = thousand) and 백 (baek = hundred) stand alone when there is just one of them.

english: You tap your card on the bus too.
tip: 도 (do = too) stacks onto other particles: 버스에서도 (beoseueseodo) = 'on the bus too'. 에서 stays put and 도 attaches right after it.

english: Is the fare to the airport expensive?
tip: 까지 (kkaji) covers both 'to' a place and 'until' a time: 공항까지 (gonghangkkaji = to the airport). One particle does the job of two English words.

english: Traffic is really bad.
tip: There is no word 'traffic' here – the road itself is blocked: 길이 많이 막혀요 (giri mani makyeoyo) = 'the road is really clogged'. That is how Koreans talk about traffic.

english: Driver, I'll get out here.
tip: 내릴게요 (naerilgeyo) uses -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) to flag an action the listener should know about – you're telling the driver you're getting off, not predicting it.

english: I paid by card.
tip: Paying is 'calculating': 카드로 계산했어요 (kadeuro gyesanhaesseoyo) = 'I calculated by card'. 계산하다 covers both doing math and settling a bill.

english: The subway is cheaper than a taxi.
tip: 보다 (boda = than) attaches to the thing you compare against: 택시보다 지하철이 싸요 (taeksiboda jihacheori ssayo) runs 'than taxis, the subway is cheap'.

english: Next month I'm going to Busan.
tip: 달 (dal) means both moon and month – 다음 달 (daeum dal = next month) is literally 'next moon', a leftover from moon-based months.

english: I'm going from Seoul to Busan by train.
tip: 에서 (eseo) and 까지 (kkaji) bracket a route as 'from...to': 서울에서 부산까지 (seoureseo busankkaji = from Seoul to Busan).

english: The next train leaves at two.
tip: Clock time mixes both number systems: hours take native numbers – 두 시 (du si = two o'clock) – while minutes switch to Sino-Korean with 분 (bun).

english: I got lost.
tip: You don't get lost in Korean – you lose the road: 길을 잃어버렸어요 (gireul ireobeoryeosseoyo) = 'I lost the way'. The road is the object, you stay the subject.

english: Excuse me, where is Myeongdong?
tip: 저기요 (jeogiyo) is literally 'over there!' – and it is the standard polite way to hail a stranger or a waiter, where English says 'excuse me'.

english: You go right from here.
tip: (으)로 marks direction: 오른쪽으로 (oreunjjogeuro = to the right).

english: Turn left at the intersection.
tip: 사거리 (sageori = intersection) — 사 (four) + 거리 (street): where four roads meet.

english: Cross the street in front of the bank.
tip: Position words come after the noun: 은행 앞에서 (eunhaeng apeseo) = 'bank front-at' = in front of the bank. 앞 (ap = front) is a noun that follows what it locates.

english: Which exit is it?
tip: Subway exits are numbered: 4번 출구 (sabeon chulgu = exit 4) — how Koreans set meeting spots.

english: I asked a subway staff member.
tip: 한테 (hante = to) marks the person you ask: 직원한테 물어봤어요 (jigwonhante mureobwasseoyo). Questions go 'to' someone – you ask to the staff, not ask the staff.

english: Now I know the way.
tip: 이제 (ije) is 'now' with a before/after edge – something changed: 이제 알아요 (ije arayo) = now I know, I didn't before. Plain 'right now' is 지금 (jigeum).

english: It took thirty minutes.
tip: Sino numbers stack: 삼십 (samsip = thirty) = 삼 (3) × 십 (10).

english: It took longer than I expected.
tip: 보다 (boda = than) attaches to abstract nouns too: 생각보다 (saenggakboda) is literally 'than thought' – the everyday way to say 'than I expected'.

english: It takes an hour by plane.
tip: 시간 (sigan = hours of duration) takes native numbers: 한 시간 (han sigan).
